steps.title: Import React and useState from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import React and the useState hook from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and useState from 'react'.
steps.seedCode: // Import React and useState from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The React library and useState hook are imported and available for use.
successCriteria: The import statement includes both React and useState from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported React and useState. This gives you access to React's core functionality and the useState hook for state management.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' package in a single import statement.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. You need to import both React and useState from the 'react' package using an import statement.

steps.title: Import useMemo and useCallback from 'react'
steps.instruction: Import the memoization hooks useMemo and useCallback from the 'react' package.
steps.hint: Add an import statement that brings in both hooks from the same package.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of importing hooks from 'react'
import { useMemo, useCallback } from 'react';
steps.seedCode:
import React, { useState } from 'react';

// Import useMemo and useCallback from 'react' here
steps.expectedOutcome: The code will have both useMemo and useCallback imported from 'react', making them available for use in the component.
successCriteria: The import statement should correctly import both useMemo and useCallback from the 'react' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported both memoization hooks from React.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close, but make sure you're importing both useMemo and useCallback from 'react'.
steps.feedbackWrong: That's not quite right. You need to import both useMemo and useCallback from the 'react' package.

steps.title: Create the main MemoizationStrategy component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named MemoizationStrategy that returns JSX.Element. Use either function declaration or arrow function syntax.
steps.hint: Define a component that returns a JSX element, like a div with some text. Remember to include the return type : JSX.Element for TypeScript.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named MemoizationStrategy is defined with a return type of JSX.Element.
successCriteria: The component is named MemoizationStrategy, returns JSX (e.g., a div or fragment), and has the correct return type annotation : JSX.Element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the MemoizationStrategy component with proper TypeScript typing.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a component, but check: Is it named exactly MemoizationStrategy? Does it return JSX? Is the return type : JSX.Element included?
steps.feedbackWrong: The component is not correctly defined. Ensure you create a functional component named MemoizationStrategy that returns JSX.Element.

steps.title: Initialize count state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside the MemoizationStrategy component, use the useState hook to create a state variable named 'count' initialized to 0.
steps.hint: Call useState with the initial value 0 and destructure the returned array into count and setCount variables.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a counter state
const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a count state variable that can be used to track and update a counter value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully initialized the count state with useState. This gives you a reactive counter value that can be updated and displayed in your component.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but there might be something missing. Make sure you're using useState with the correct syntax: const [count, setCount] = useState<number>(0);
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look quite right. You need to initialize a state variable named 'count' with an initial value of 0 using the useState hook.

steps.title: Initialize multiplier state with useState
steps.instruction: Inside the MemoizationStrategy component, use useState to create a state variable named 'multiplier' and initialize it to the number 2.
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with a generic type <number> and an initial value of 2.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of initializing a number state
const [multiplier, setMultiplier] = useState<number>(2);
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a multiplier state variable that can be used later for calculations.
successCriteria: The code should include a useState call that declares a 'multiplier' variable with an initial value of 2.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the multiplier state with the correct initial value.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but check that you've named the variable 'multiplier' and initialized it to 2.
steps.feedbackWrong: Please use useState to create a state variable named 'multiplier' initialized to 2.

steps.title: Create an expensive calculation function
steps.instruction: Inside the MemoizationStrategy component, create a function called expensiveCalculation that takes a number parameter and returns a computed value. This function should simulate expensive computation.
steps.hint: Define a function with the signature (num: number) => number. You can perform a simple calculation like multiplication or addition to simulate computation.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have an expensiveCalculation function defined inside your component that takes a number and returns a computed value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created the expensiveCalculation function. This function simulates expensive computation that we'll later optimize with memoization.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function: 1) is named 'expensiveCalculation', 2) takes a number parameter, 3) returns a number value, and 4) is defined inside the component.
steps.feedbackWrong: The expensiveCalculation function isn't quite right. Remember to create a function inside the component that takes a number and returns a computed value.

steps.title: Memoize the expensive calculation with useMemo
steps.instruction: Inside your component, create a memoizedResult variable using useMemo that calls expensiveCalculation with the current count value.
steps.hint: Call useMemo with a function that returns expensiveCalculation(count), and pass [count] as the dependency array.
steps.expectedOutcome: The expensive calculation will be memoized and only recomputed when count changes.
successCriteria: expensiveCalculation(count) is inside the useMemo callback
Result is assigned to memoizedResult variable
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully memoized the expensive calculation. The result will now be cached and only recalculated when count changes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're calling useMemo with a function that returns expensiveCalculation(count), and that you include [count] as the dependency array.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's focus on using useMemo. You need to create a memoizedResult variable that calls useMemo with a function returning expensiveCalculation(count), and pass [count] as the dependency array.

steps.title: Create a non-memoized calculation for comparison
steps.instruction: Create a regularResult variable that calls expensiveCalculation with count directly (without memoization).
steps.hint: Define a variable named regularResult and assign it the result of calling expensiveCalculation(count).
steps.analogousExample:
// Example of a non-memoized calculation
const regularResult = expensiveCalculation(count);
steps.expectedOutcome: A regularResult variable that stores the result of expensiveCalculation(count) for comparison with the memoized version.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a non-memoized calculation that will help demonstrate the performance difference.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling expensiveCalculation with count as the argument and storing it in a variable named regularResult.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a variable called regularResult that calls expensiveCalculation(count) directly.

steps.title: Create an event handler with useCallback
steps.instruction: Inside your MemoizationStrategy component, create a handleIncrement function using useCallback that increments the count state by 1.
steps.hint: Use useCallback to memoize the function. The callback should call setCount with the current count plus 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a memoized handleIncrement function that increments the count state.
successCriteria: The handleIncrement function should be defined using useCallback, call setCount to increment count by 1, and have an empty dependency array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully created a memoized event handler using useCallback. This will prevent unnecessary re-creations of the function on each render.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're using useCallback correctly. The function should call setCount to increment count by 1 and have an empty dependency array.
steps.feedbackWrong: That doesn't look right. Remember to use useCallback to create a memoized function that increments the count state.

steps.title: Create a regular event handler for comparison
steps.instruction: Create a regular (non-memoized) function named handleMultiplier that increments the multiplier state by 1 when called.
steps.hint: Define a function inside your component that calls setMultiplier with the current multiplier value plus 1.
steps.expectedOutcome: A regular function handleMultiplier that increments the multiplier state by 1.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a regular event handler that increments the multiplier state. This will serve as a comparison point for the memoized handler you'll create next.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your handleMultiplier function properly increments the multiplier state by 1 when called.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try creating a function called handleMultiplier that uses setMultiplier to increase the multiplier value by 1.

steps.title: Add the main JSX structure
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add the main JSX structure: a div containing headings and sections to display results. Start by adding a section with a heading for the memoized calculation results.
steps.hint: Add JSX elements inside the existing div. You can start with a section element containing an h2 heading.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a basic JSX structure with a main heading and a section for displaying results.
successCriteria: Add at least one section element
Add at least one heading (h2, h3, etc.) inside the section
Structure should be inside the existing div
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added the basic JSX structure. This provides the foundation for displaying the memoization results.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some JSX, but make sure you have a section element with a heading inside it.
steps.feedbackWrong: The JSX structure wasn't added correctly. Make sure to add a section element with a heading inside the existing div.

steps.title: Add buttons and display results
steps.instruction: Inside the component's return statement, add two buttons and display the memoized and non-memoized calculation results. Add a button to increment count (with onClick={handleIncrement}) and a button to update multiplier (with onClick={handleMultiplier}). Display memoizedResult and a non-memoized calculation call.
steps.hint: Add the buttons and result displays inside the existing div. Use the handlers and variables already defined in previous steps.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have interactive buttons to update state and display both memoized and non-memoized calculation results.
successCriteria: The return statement must include: 1) A button with onClick={handleIncrement} and text 'Increment Count', 2) A button with onClick={handleMultiplier} and text 'Update Multiplier', 3) A paragraph displaying memoizedResult, 4) A paragraph displaying nonMemoizedResult.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added the buttons and result displays. The UI now shows both memoized and non-memoized calculations, allowing users to see the performance difference.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some elements, but make sure you have both buttons (with correct onClick handlers) and both result displays (memoizedResult and nonMemoizedResult).
steps.feedbackWrong: The UI elements are missing or incorrect. Check that you've added both buttons with their onClick handlers and both result paragraphs.
